item.title: How to Stop Your Phone From Overheating While Charging
item.description: Phone hot while charging? Learn why it happens, which habits actually help, and the settings and gear that keep battery temps down.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Last summer I left a Pixel 7 on a hotel nightstand, plugged into a 30W brick under a pillow, and came back 40 minutes later to a phone so hot the case had softened and Android had thrown a temperature warning. The battery drained 6% that night even though it was plugged in — heat kills charging efficiency, and the phone had throttled itself to protect the cell.

That’s the thing most people miss: a phone that’s hot while charging isn’t just uncomfortable. It’s actively damaging the one part you can’t replace cheaply. A lithium-ion battery held at 45°C (113°F) for extended periods ages measurably faster than one kept at 25–30°C. You won’t see it this week. You’ll see it in 14 months when your phone dies at 20%.

Here’s what actually causes the heat, what doesn’t, and the specific steps that drop temperatures.

Why phones get hot while charging

Charging is not 100% efficient. Roughly 10–20% of the energy flowing into the phone is lost as heat, and that loss happens in two places: the charging brick (which converts AC wall power to DC) and inside the phone itself (the charging IC and the battery).

The physics is simple. Power (watts) = voltage × current. Push 45W into a phone and you’re moving a lot of energy through small components. Fast charging deliberately raises voltage and current, which raises heat. That’s the tradeoff nobody advertises: 0–50% in 20 minutes comes with a warmer phone than 0–50% in 45 minutes.

Three heat sources stack on top of each other:

  1. The charging process itself — unavoidable, but manageable.
  2. The phone working while charging — screen on, games, navigation, hotspot, background sync.
  3. The environment — ambient temperature, insulation from cases, surfaces that trap heat.

Most overheating complaints are sources 2 and 3, not the charger.

The single biggest mistake: charging under a pillow, in bed, or in a car dock

If you only fix one thing, fix this.

A phone under a pillow has essentially zero airflow. I’ve measured a Galaxy S23 charging on a bed versus the same phone on a bare desk: the bed version ran 8–11°C hotter within 30 minutes. That’s the difference between “warm” and “Android is limiting charging speed.”

The car is worse. A phone in a windshield mount on a sunny day, running Google Maps and charging at 15W, sits in an environment that can hit 50°C before the phone even starts working. Dash-mounted phones in summer routinely trigger thermal shutdowns.

Do this instead: charge on a hard, cool surface — a desk, a nightstand, a countertop. Wood and metal are fine. Fabric, bedding, couch cushions, and closed car gloveboxes are not.

The step-by-step checklist

Run through this in order. Most people find their problem in the first three items.

1. Take the case off for fast charges. Thick cases — OtterBox Defenders, wallet cases, anything with a metal plate for a magnetic mount — trap heat against the back glass. A 2mm TPU case is fine. A rugged case adds 3–5°C during a 30W charge. If your phone is already hot, pop the case.

2. Match the charger to the phone. A 65W laptop charger doesn’t force 65W into a phone that only accepts 25W. USB-C negotiation handles that. But a cheap no-name brick that doesn’t properly negotiate can push inefficient voltage and run hot itself. Use the charger that came in the box, or a reputable one from Anker, Ugreen, Google, Samsung, or Apple.

3. Stop using the phone while it charges. This is the one people ignore. Gaming while plugged in is the worst case: a Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 under load draws 8–12W on its own, plus 20W+ from charging. That’s 30W of heat generation in a device with no fan. If you must use it, keep the screen brightness low and avoid games, video calls, and navigation.

4. Turn on the right settings. On iPhone: Settings → Battery → Charging → turn on Optimized Battery Charging. On Android: Settings → Battery → Adaptive Charging or Battery Protection (Samsung calls it “Protect battery,” which caps charge at 85%). These slow the final 20% of charging, which is the hottest phase.

5. Kill background activity during charge. Hotspot, Bluetooth tethering, cloud photo backup, and app updates all run the processor. On Android, enable Airplane Mode with Wi-Fi on if you don’t need calls. On iPhone, Low Power Mode reduces background refresh.

6. Charge in a cool room. Charging in a 30°C room versus a 22°C room makes a measurable difference. Don’t charge on a windowsill in direct sun or on top of a running appliance.

7. Don’t charge overnight on a fast charger if you don’t need to. Slow 5W charging overnight generates far less heat. If you have an old 5W brick in a drawer, use it for the 11pm–7am charge and save fast charging for when you’re awake.

8. Check for a failing battery or bad cable. A swollen battery, a battery reporting below 80% health, or a frayed cable with a damaged connector can all cause abnormal heat. A cable that’s warm to the touch near the plug is a fire risk — replace it.

What most guides get wrong

Myth 1: “Closing all your apps stops the phone from overheating while charging.” This is mostly wrong on modern phones. iOS and Android aggressively suspend background apps. Force-closing 20 apps does almost nothing for charging temperature. What actually matters is whether an app is actively running a foreground process — navigation, a game, a video call, a hotspot. Close those. Leave the rest alone.

Myth 2: “Fast charging destroys your battery, so always use a slow charger.” Fast charging does generate more heat, but it’s not the villain it’s made out to be. Phones manage it: they charge fast to about 50–60%, then taper hard. The real damage comes from heat combined with high charge states. A phone fast-charging from 20% to 60% on a desk stays cooler than a phone slow-charging from 90% to 100% under a pillow. The conditions matter more than the wattage.

Myth 3: “Wireless charging is gentler.” Wireless charging is typically 60–75% efficient, versus 85–90% for wired. That missing energy becomes heat — in the phone and in the pad. A 15W MagSafe charge can run hotter than a 20W wired charge because so much power is lost in the coil gap. If your phone overheats on a wireless pad, that’s why. Thick cases make it worse by increasing the gap.

When to worry — and when not to

A phone that’s warm to the touch during fast charging is normal. A phone that’s hot — uncomfortable to hold, showing a temperature warning, or refusing to charge past 80% — is not.

Concrete thresholds:

  • Under 35°C (95°F): Normal. No action needed.
  • 35–40°C: Warm. Check your setup — case, surface, background apps.
  • 40–45°C: Hot. Stop fast charging, remove the case, close heavy apps.
  • Above 45°C: The phone will throttle or stop charging. Unplug it and let it cool to room temperature before charging again.

You can check battery temperature on Android with apps like AccuBattery or DevCheck. On iPhone, there’s no direct readout, but a “Temperature” warning in Settings → Battery, or the phone dimming its screen and refusing to charge, means you’re past the limit.

The gear that actually helps

If you charge a lot and want to solve this properly:

  • A charger with good thermal design. Anker’s Nano II series and Ugreen’s Nexode line run cooler than generic bricks because they use GaN (gallium nitride) components, which waste less energy as heat. A 30W GaN brick is roughly the size of an old 5W iPhone charger and stays noticeably cooler.
  • A stand that lifts the phone off the surface. Any cheap wire stand improves airflow to the back panel. This is the single cheapest fix.
  • A cable rated for the current. A 3A cable on a 5A charger creates resistance and heat at the connector. Match the cable to the charger.
  • A cooling pad for heavy use. If you game while charging — and you probably shouldn’t — a small USB fan pointed at the back of the phone drops surface temps by 5–8°C in my testing.

The bottom line

Phone overheating while charging is almost always a setup problem, not a hardware defect. Move it off the bed. Take the case off for fast charges. Don’t game while plugged in. Use a decent charger and a cable that matches it. Enable the battery-protection setting your phone already has.

Do those five things and you’ll drop charging temperatures by 5–10°C, which is the difference between a battery that lasts three years and one that’s begging for a replacement at 18 months. The heat you feel today is the capacity you lose next year.

item.title: How to Clean a Laptop Keyboard Without Breaking It
item.description: Learn how to clean a laptop keyboard safely with tools you already own, plus fixes for sticky keys, crumbs, and spills.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Last month a client handed me a laptop with a spacebar that only registered one out of every four presses. She’d been living with it for six weeks because she assumed the keyboard was failing and a repair would cost $120. It wasn’t failing. A single popcorn kernel fragment had wedged under the keycap and was blocking the scissor mechanism underneath. Ten minutes with a can of compressed air and a plastic spudger fixed it, and she didn’t pay me anything because I was already there for a software issue.

That story repeats constantly. Most laptop keyboards don’t break from use. They break from what falls into them, and most of what falls in can be removed at home with the right technique. The catch is that laptop keyboards are not desktop keyboards. You can’t yank a keycap off a MacBook the way you can on a $40 mechanical board and expect it to snap back. The tolerances are tighter, the mechanisms are thinner, and one wrong move turns a cleaning job into a $200 top-case replacement.

This guide covers what actually works, what quietly destroys keyboards, and how to handle the two situations that scare people most: sticky keys and liquid spills.

First, Know What You’re Dealing With

Before you touch anything, identify your keyboard type. It changes your entire approach.

Chiclet/scissor-switch keyboards (MacBooks, most modern ultrabooks, Dell XPS, ThinkPads): flat keys with minimal travel, held by a plastic scissor mechanism under each cap. These are the most common and the most fragile. Individual keycaps can be reattached, but the tiny clips snap easily.

Membrane keyboards (budget laptops, older machines): a rubber dome sheet under the keys. Dirt tends to sit on top rather than fall through, but liquid damage is worse because the membrane traps it.

Mechanical laptop keyboards (rare, some gaming laptops): individual switches, more forgiving, but still not designed for frequent cap removal.

If you’re unsure, search your exact model plus “keycap removal” before proceeding. Two minutes of research prevents a broken clip.

The Tools That Actually Work (and Three That Don’t)

You need less than you think. Here’s the honest list.

Get these:

  • Compressed air can with a straw nozzle, or better, a rubber bulb blower (no propellant, no moisture risk)
  • 90% or higher isopropyl alcohol
  • Microfiber cloths, at least two
  • Soft-bristle brush, like a clean makeup brush or an anti-static brush
  • Plastic spudger or a guitar pick
  • Wooden toothpicks
  • Optional: a keycap puller if your model supports it

Avoid these:

  • Household wipes and glass cleaner. They leave residue that attracts more dust and can strip the anti-glare coating on nearby surfaces.
  • Vacuum cleaners with brush attachments. The static buildup can damage internal components, and the suction can rip keycaps off.
  • Cotton swabs dipped in liquid. The cotton sheds fibers into the gaps, and excess liquid drips where you can’t reach it.

The 15-Minute Routine Clean (Do This Monthly)

This is your maintenance protocol. It handles 90% of everyday grime without removing a single keycap.

Step 1: Power down and unplug. Shut the laptop completely. Not sleep. Off. Unplug the charger and any peripherals. This prevents accidental keystrokes and eliminates any electrical risk.

Step 2: Turn it upside down and shake gently. Hold it at a 45-degree angle over a trash can and tap the bottom firmly a few times. You’ll be surprised how much debris falls out before you’ve done anything else.

Step 3: Blow air in short bursts at an angle. Hold the can upright, attach the straw, and use bursts of one to two seconds. Aim at a 45-degree angle across the keys, not straight down. Straight-down blasts push debris deeper. Work in rows, left to right, then right to left.

Critical warning: never shake a compressed air can while spraying, and never spray so long that the can frosts over. That frost is propellant, and it leaves wet residue.

Step 4: Dry-brush the surface. Use your soft brush in the same angled motion to lift dust the air loosened. Brush toward the edges of the keyboard, not into the gaps.

Step 5: Wipe with a barely damp cloth. Dampen a microfiber cloth with isopropyl alcohol, then wring it so it’s nearly dry. Wipe across the keys. The alcohol evaporates in seconds and kills the bacteria that make keyboards smell.

Step 6: Dry completely before closing the lid. Wait two full minutes. Closing a lid on residual moisture traps it against the screen.

When Keys Are Sticky or Unresponsive

A sticky key means something is physically blocking the mechanism. Here’s the escalation ladder, from least to most invasive.

Level 1: The toothpick pass. Slide a wooden toothpick along all four sides of the offending key, angling it under the cap edge. You’re fishing for crumbs and lint. Do this over a trash can.

Level 2: Targeted air blast. Tilt the laptop so the sticky key is the lowest point and blast air from the highest edge, pushing debris downhill and out.

Level 3: The alcohol flush (use sparingly). Put two or three drops of 90% isopropyl alcohol directly at the base of the key, then press the key 20 to 30 times rapidly. The alcohol dissolves sticky residue from spilled soda or juice. Wait 30 minutes before using the laptop. Do not do this on more than one or two keys at a time.

Level 4: Keycap removal. Only attempt this if you’ve confirmed your model supports it. Insert the spudger under one corner, apply gentle upward pressure, and work around the cap. Never pry from the center. Photograph the scissor mechanism before you lift the cap so you know how it reassembles. Reinstall by aligning the cap’s clips and pressing straight down until you hear a soft click.

If a key still doesn’t work after Level 4, the switch itself is likely damaged. That’s a hardware repair, not a cleaning problem.

The Liquid Spill Protocol (Act in 10 Seconds)

Spills are the one case where speed beats technique.

  1. Unplug immediately and power off. If it won’t power off, hold the power button for 10 seconds.
  2. Flip the laptop upside down into a tent shape so liquid drains away from the internals instead of deeper in.
  3. Blot, don’t wipe. Press a microfiber cloth onto the keyboard. Wiping spreads liquid into adjacent keys.
  4. Do not turn it on. Not in an hour. Not tomorrow. Water and sugary drinks need 48 to 72 hours to fully dry, and powering on a wet board causes short circuits.
  5. If it was anything other than water, you need professional cleaning. Sugary and acidic liquids leave conductive residue that corrodes traces over weeks.

Here’s the part most people get wrong: a laptop that turns on after a spill is not necessarily fine. Corrosion is slow. I’ve seen machines fail three weeks after a coffee spill that seemed harmless on day one.

Five Mistakes That Cost People Real Money

Using too much liquid. A damp cloth means damp. If you can wring a drop out of it, it’s too wet.

Spraying cleaner directly on the keyboard. It pools in the gaps and migrates to the motherboard. Always apply to the cloth first.

Pressing keys while cleaning. You’re pushing debris past the membrane and into the contact layer.

Removing all the keycaps at once. You will forget the layout, and the clips are model-specific. One or two keys at a time, maximum.

Skipping the screen and vents. Dust pulled from the keyboard often settles into the vents. Clean those in the same session or you’re just relocating the problem.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Power off, unplug charger and peripherals
  • Turn upside down, tap gently over trash
  • Short bursts of air at 45-degree angle
  • Soft brush from center toward edges
  • Microfiber cloth damp with 90% isopropyl alcohol
  • Toothpick pass on any sticky keys
  • Wait 2 minutes before closing lid
  • Clean vents and screen in the same session
  • For spills: power off, tent upside down, wait 48-72 hours

How Often You Actually Need to Do This

Monthly for the routine clean if you eat near your laptop. Every three months if you don’t. Deep clean with keycap removal only when a specific key misbehaves, not on a schedule. And if you’re a heavy snacker, a $15 silicone keyboard cover will save you hours of this work, though it does change the typing feel and traps heat on some models.

The keyboard on your laptop is one of the few components you touch every single day. Fifteen minutes a month keeps it responsive, sanitary, and out of the repair shop. That’s a trade worth making.

item.title: How to Back Up Your Phone Data: A Complete Guide
item.description: Learn how to back up phone data safely on iPhone and Android. Compare cloud, computer, and SIM methods with step-by-step instructions.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Last year, a friend of mine dropped her iPhone into a lake during a camping trip. Two years of photos, her kids’ first steps, voice memos from her late father — gone in seconds. She hadn’t backed up a single thing because she “kept meaning to do it.” Don’t be my friend.

Your phone holds more of your life than any filing cabinet ever did. Photos, contacts, banking apps, two-factor authentication codes, work documents, and years of text conversations. Losing it isn’t just inconvenient — it can take weeks to fully recover, and some things never come back.

The good news? Backing up your phone takes about 15 minutes to set up and a few minutes per week to maintain. Here’s exactly how to do it, whether you’re on iPhone or Android.

Why You Should Back Up More Than Once

Before we get into the how, let’s talk about the why behind redundancy.

A single backup is better than nothing, but it’s still a single point of failure. Cloud accounts get locked. External drives fail. Phones get stolen along with the bag holding your backup drive. The smartest approach is the 3-2-1 rule: three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with one copy stored off-site (cloud counts).

In practice, that means:

  • Cloud backup for convenience and automatic updates
  • Local backup on a computer or external drive for speed and full control
  • Critical files (like photos) also synced to a separate service

You don’t need to be paranoid. You just need two methods running in parallel.

How to Back Up an iPhone

Apple gives you two solid options: iCloud and a computer. Use both if you can.

Method 1: iCloud Backup

This is the set-it-and-forget-it option.

  1. Connect your iPhone to Wi-Fi and plug it into a charger.
  2. Go to Settings → [Your Name] → iCloud → iCloud Backup.
  3. Toggle Back Up This iPhone on.
  4. Tap Back Up Now for the first run.

From then on, your iPhone backs up automatically once a day when it’s locked, charging, and on Wi-Fi. Free accounts get 5GB, which fills up fast. Photos and videos alone can eat that in a week. If you’re serious about backups, the 50GB tier ($0.99/month) is worth it for most people.

What iCloud backs up: app data, photos, messages, contacts, calendar, settings, health data, and more. What it doesn’t back up: anything already synced to iCloud separately (like iCloud Photos), plus content from apps that use their own servers.

Method 2: Back Up to a Mac or PC

This gives you a full, encrypted local copy — including saved passwords and Wi-Fi networks that iCloud sometimes skips.

On a Mac (macOS Catalina or later):

  1. Connect your iPhone with a cable.
  2. Open Finder and select your device in the sidebar.
  3. Click Back Up Now.
  4. Check Encrypt local backup if you want passwords and health data included. Set a password you’ll remember — Apple can’t recover it.

On Windows:

  1. Install iTunes if you don’t have it.
  2. Connect your iPhone, open iTunes, and click the phone icon.
  3. Choose This Computer and click Back Up Now.

Pro tip: Back up to an external drive if your laptop’s storage is tight. iPhone backups can easily hit 100GB+.

How to Back Up an Android Phone

Android’s backup situation is more fragmented because manufacturers customize the operating system. But the core tools are solid.

Method 1: Google One Backup

This is the Android equivalent of iCloud.

  1. Open Settings → Google → Backup (or search “backup” in settings).
  2. Make sure Back up to Google Drive is on.
  3. Tap Back up now.

Google gives you 15GB free across Drive, Gmail, and Photos. That’s more generous than Apple, but still tight if you shoot a lot of video.

What it backs up: apps and app data, call history, contacts, device settings, SMS messages, and photos/videos (if Google Photos backup is enabled).

What it doesn’t: files in your Downloads folder, some third-party app data, and anything stored locally outside standard directories.

Method 2: Manufacturer Tools

Samsung, Xiaomi, OnePlus, and others offer their own backup utilities:

  • Samsung Smart Switch — backs up to a PC, Mac, or external drive
  • Xiaomi Mi Mover — transfers between Xiaomi devices
  • OnePlus Switch — similar functionality

These are especially useful when migrating to a new phone, since they preserve app layouts and settings that Google’s backup misses.

Method 3: Manual File Transfer

For photos, videos, and documents, sometimes the simplest method wins. Plug your Android into a computer via USB, set the connection mode to File Transfer, and drag your DCIM, Downloads, and Documents folders onto your hard drive.

It’s not elegant. It works every time.

Don’t Forget These Often-Missed Items

Standard backups cover the basics, but a few things slip through the cracks:

  • WhatsApp chats — back up separately inside the app (Settings → Chats → Chat Backup). These don’t always ride along with your phone backup.
  • Two-factor authentication apps — Google Authenticator and similar apps often don’t back up. If you lose your phone, you could be locked out of everything. Export your codes or switch to an app with cloud sync.
  • Photos in “Recently Deleted” — these won’t transfer. Empty the folder only after confirming your backup includes what you need.
  • Voice memos and notes — check that your notes app syncs to the cloud. Apple Notes and Google Keep do; some third-party apps don’t.
  • Saved passwords — use a password manager (Bitwarden, 1Password, or your browser’s built-in vault) rather than relying on phone backup alone.

How Often Should You Back Up?

Here’s a simple schedule that covers most people:

  • Daily: Automatic cloud backup (set it and forget it)
  • Weekly: Verify the backup actually completed — check the timestamp
  • Monthly: Run a full local backup to a computer or external drive
  • Before any major change: Phone upgrade, factory reset, or OS update

The weekly check matters more than people realize. Backups fail silently all the time — usually because of full cloud storage or a Wi-Fi hiccup. A 30-second glance at the backup date saves a lot of grief.

A Quick Word on Encryption

If you’re backing up locally, always enable encryption. An unencrypted phone backup on a laptop or external drive is a goldmine for anyone who gets their hands on it — passwords, messages, banking app data, everything.

For cloud backups, encryption is handled by Apple and Google, though neither offers end-to-end encryption by default for phone backups. If that concerns you, consider tools like Cryptomator for sensitive files, or back up locally with encryption enabled.

Final Thoughts

Backing up your phone isn’t a one-time task — it’s a habit. Set up automatic cloud backup today, do a local backup this weekend, and check both once a week. That’s it.

The 15 minutes you spend now could save you from the kind of data loss that no recovery service can fix. Ask my friend about the lake sometime. She’ll tell you the same thing.

item.title: How to Speed Up Your Computer: 12 Proven Fixes That Work
item.description: Is your PC crawling? Learn how to speed up your computer with 12 practical fixes, from startup cleanup to hardware upgrades that actually deliver.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Last month, a friend handed me her laptop and said, “It takes four minutes just to open Chrome.” Four minutes. She’d been living with it for over a year, assuming she needed to buy a new machine. Twenty minutes of work later—no new hardware, no reinstall—her boot time dropped to under 30 seconds.

That’s the thing about slow computers: the fix is usually simpler than people think. Most slowdowns come from a handful of fixable problems—bloatware hogging resources, a full hard drive, outdated drivers, or background apps you forgot existed.

This guide walks through 12 fixes in order of impact. Start at the top, work your way down, and stop when your machine feels fast again. Most people solve 80% of their problem with the first four.

Why Computers Slow Down Over Time

Hardware doesn’t degrade the way people assume. A 2018 processor runs just as fast today as it did new. What changes is everything around it:

  • Startup programs multiply every time you install software
  • Storage fills up, and drives get slower as they approach capacity
  • Background processes accumulate—updaters, sync tools, telemetry
  • Operating systems get heavier with each major update
  • Dust and heat cause thermal throttling on laptops
  • Malware quietly consumes resources

Understanding this matters because it tells you where to look. You’re not fighting entropy—you’re cleaning up specific, identifiable messes.

Quick Wins (Do These First)

1. Trim Your Startup Programs

This is the single highest-impact fix for most people.

Windows: Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager, go to the Startup tab, and disable anything you don’t need running the moment you log in. Be aggressive. Spotify, Steam, Slack, Adobe Creative Cloud, and most “helper” utilities don’t need to launch at boot.

Mac: Go to System Settings → General → Login Items and remove what you don’t need.

Don’t disable your antivirus, audio drivers, or touchpad software. Everything else is fair game—you can always re-enable it.

2. Uninstall Software You Don’t Use

Open your installed programs list and sort by size or install date. You’ll find things you installed once for a single task in 2021. Every installed program adds registry entries, background services, and update checkers.

On Windows, check Settings → Apps → Installed Apps. On Mac, drag unused apps from Applications to the Trash, then empty it.

3. Free Up Disk Space

Both Windows and macOS slow down noticeably when your system drive is above 90% full. The operating system needs room for virtual memory and temporary files.

Aim to keep at least 15% of your drive free. Quick ways to reclaim space:

  • Run Disk Cleanup (Windows) or check Storage in System Settings (Mac)
  • Clear browser caches—Chrome alone can accumulate 10+ GB
  • Move large media files to an external drive or cloud storage
  • Delete old downloads and duplicate photos

4. Restart Properly

Not sleep. Not hibernate. An actual shutdown and restart. Windows especially benefits because a full restart clears memory leaks and applies pending updates. If you only ever close the lid, try shutting down once a week and see the difference.

Deeper Fixes for Stubborn Slowness

5. Check for Malware

If your computer got slow suddenly rather than gradually, malware is a real possibility. Run a full scan with Windows Defender (it’s genuinely good now) or Malwarebytes. On Mac, Malwarebytes for Mac catches adware that most people don’t realize they have.

6. Update Your Drivers and OS

Outdated graphics drivers cause stuttering in games and video playback. Outdated chipset drivers cause general sluggishness. Windows Update handles most of this, but GPU drivers are worth updating manually from NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel’s site.

On Mac, keep macOS current—Apple’s updates often include performance fixes.

7. Reduce Visual Effects

Windows animations look nice but cost resources on older hardware.

Go to System Properties → Advanced → Performance Settings and choose “Adjust for best performance,” or manually disable animations you don’t care about. The difference is noticeable on machines with integrated graphics.

8. Manage Browser Bloat

Your browser might be the actual bottleneck, not your computer. Extensions are the usual culprit—each one runs code on every page you visit.

  • Audit your extensions and remove anything you haven’t used in a month
  • Limit yourself to 10-15 open tabs, or use a tab suspension extension
  • Clear cache and cookies periodically
  • Try a lighter browser if Chrome feels heavy

9. Disable Unnecessary Background Services

Windows runs dozens of services you’ll never use—print spooler if you don’t print, fax service, Xbox Game Bar if you don’t game. Type services.msc in the Run dialog and set rarely-used services to Manual rather than Automatic.

Be careful here. If you’re unsure what a service does, look it up before touching it.

Hardware Upgrades That Actually Pay Off

10. Swap Your Hard Drive for an SSD

If your computer still has a mechanical hard drive, this is the upgrade. Nothing else comes close. An SSD can cut boot time from minutes to seconds and make everything feel instant.

A 500GB SSD costs $40-60. Cloning software is often included free. If you have a laptop from 2015 or later, it almost certainly supports one.

11. Add More RAM

8GB is the practical minimum for modern Windows; 16GB is comfortable. If you regularly see memory usage above 80% in Task Manager, more RAM will help. Check your motherboard’s specs first—laptops often have one or two accessible slots.

12. Clean Out the Dust

This sounds trivial until you see a laptop heatsink packed solid with dust. When components overheat, they throttle—running slower to avoid damage. Open the case (or the laptop’s bottom panel), blow out dust with compressed air, and make sure fans spin freely.

When to Stop Fixing and Start Replacing

If you’ve done all of the above and your computer is still slow, consider the math. A 10-year-old machine with a dual-core processor and 4GB of RAM has limits no software tweak can overcome. But if your computer is less than six or seven years old, these fixes will almost always bring it back to usable speed.

The Bottom Line

Speed up your computer by attacking the biggest offenders first: startup programs, disk space, and malware. Then move to drivers, browser cleanup, and visual settings. If you’re still stuck, an SSD upgrade is the best money you can spend on an older machine.

Start with Task Manager’s startup tab right now. It takes two minutes, and it’s the fix that helps most people the most.
